title: ClawLabs：从个人编码走向共享智能体
author: OpenAI
content:
Brief Description

The ClawLabs team explains its move from individual coding sessions to persistent collaborative agents, demonstrates shared artifacts and community workflows, and introduces deployment controls and an open-source agent platform.

Table of Contents

  • From Terminal Sessions to Collaborative Agents
  • Building a Game Together
  • Reviewing Intent and Collaborative Workflows
  • Artifacts, Prompts, and Agent-Driven Design
  • Persistent Maintenance and Shared Experiments
  • Deployment Controls and Scaling Agents
  • Permissions and Community Agent Demonstrations
  • ClawLabs and Open-Source Infrastructure

From Terminal Sessions to Collaborative Agents

Let's talk, we have a really exciting session today. I'm going to show you what I learned over the year maintaining my open source projects, how my workflows evolved, and what happened when we moved development of OpenClaw to OC itself. Now, let's talk a little bit about the harnesses we use to talk to our agent.

This whole year, this whole revolution started in the CLI. Last year, I was fully living in the terminal. Split screen, lots of Codex sessions, my code was flying around left and right.

And then over time, the models got better and smarter. And the time where I had to smash escape to steer the agent decreased. It's not really needed anymore.

It was clear my workflow needed a change. Then I moved to Codex Desktop. Now the chat should be there.

It made it far easier to start a large number of sessions concurrently.

The text is easier to read. It has visualization. It has an inline browser.

It has really code review. I don't even know. It's nice.

Now that it's so easy to run all these sessions and experiments, my machine was dying. I ran out of disk space. My fans sounded like a jet engine.

So I started using multiple computers to run more work. I connected Codex to DevBoxes. So I could spread the load.

And I built Grabboxes so agents would run the tests in the cloud. I think I'd peek ahead, I don't know, six or ten machines that were crunching through all my code and my experiments. Sometimes in one Codex and sometimes they used VNC.

And then I realized that was a problem all these machines wouldn't solve. When my teammates wanted to get involved, they still had to come through me. we were all working with agents, but we weren't really working together.

By the way, I love this slide. It's that's how tokens look? Frank Allenby, he coined this term this year, meat proxy. what I'm talking about.

Let's not be a meat proxy. That's when you are the interface to AI and you pass messages back and forth. So how does the rest of the team get involved?

How do you see what it's doing, understand the decisions, and help move the work forward? That's what we started exploring as we began using OC to build OC. And for those of you who haven't used it, OpenClaw is an open source platform for persistent agents.

It works across your tools, your devices, your teams. You can sign in with your subscription. There's now a fancy sign in with ChatGPT button.

It picks up your plugins, and you can even see your Codex sessions. Also let's talk about governance.

OpenClaw is open source, and it's owned by the OpenClaw Foundation, an independent nonprofit. And OpenAI generously supports our mission. My team at OpenAI explores how to design agents that are useful, how to run them at scale, how they can help us improve both our work and our personal lives.

And ultimately also how an automated software engineer could look like. My thesis is that the models are getting so good so fast. The way we work, the way our harnesses work, we just can't keep up.

Workflows that made sense a year ago, or even six months ago, already feel constrained and outdated. Now, part of my work is to explore where things go. Should we take a look?

You already saw that the demo gods love us today. So let's see if PartyClaw is online. Hey PartyClaw, are you alive?

Well, the voice translation works, even though it's not perfect.

Building a Game Together

Will I manage?

Think about you doing open source and you want to work with a team. And we used to have pull requests to collaborate, but that just feels not the future anymore. So here on the server, anyone can see each other session.

You can prompt each other session. It's meant for people that work together. Don't invite anyone who you don't want to mess with your sessions.

We're going to use this in the future as we build OpenClaw to invite some of our top contributors. you get the tokens and we get a little bit of your ideas. I think it's an amazing deal. And this whole workshop, this idea, this is really to get you thinking.

Which other workflows do we currently do in the old way that we could do so much better in this agentic age? Oh, I think my lobster game is ready. Oh, it's lobsters and sharks now?

Okay. Oh, it died. Damn it.

Well, while you all are having fun here, and oh, my God, how many people did we let in? We need to close the gates, guys. Yeah, you already see that stuff's happening.

We're going to check back later on this. Let's switch back to the slides. So, you just saw us working a little bit together on a game.

Now, we started experimenting with how would multiplayer work with agents a few months ago. And it has changed how we work as a team. Not only has it increased velocity, it also just made us happier. there's so many conflicts that you can avoid if you see each other's prompts.

And now it feels like we're actually more working like a team.

Reviewing Intent and Collaborative Workflows

And earlier today, you saw dots, which is a really cool first-party integration of the OpenAI experience for companies to work with agents. OpenClaw explores some of the same ideas. Agents working alongside a whole team of people.

OpenClaw gives you the freedom to choose your model, change the code, and you can fully run it on your own infrastructure. And I think we should celebrate that. I love that OpenAI is supporting all these different approaches.

And that the open source community can take these ideas in directions we haven't even imagined. And of course, we're really thinking about ways how your dots can talk to your claw and vice versa. Now, one thing I didn't talk about is your prompts.

A single sentence can now produce thousands or tens of thousands of lines of code. But the conversation behind it often stays on someone's local machine.

I reviewed so many PRs where I understood what changed, but not why. show me the prompt. So I tried this. I added a skill that asked people to send a sanitized version of the transcript and attach it to the PR.

And very few said yes. Sharing how you talk to your agent feels surprisingly personal. Heck, even I sometimes said no.

I don't know. You know? So when we made sessions visible to the whole team, it did feel awkward for a day.

We were reading each other's conversations. We laughed a little. And then it became the new normal.

And now we learn from each other. And we catch mistakes earlier. Let me show you how it looks like.

So, the demo gods are still on our side. And I imagine I wake up. I didn't have my coffee yet.

And I see this pull request from Roboclaw. And I scroll through it.

And there, somebody changed how tables look and made them smaller. But I did the same work. And I made them bigger just the day before. like my cortisol level would go up.

It's who did this? Like, why? What did Victor do?

And maybe in the past, I would have dropped him a not very Californian message. But now, I can click on the work session. And I can just check out what he did, right?

And it actually looks like he reused my session. Or he even pinged me. I should read my emails more often.

I love this. See this? We were just talking about how we talked to our agents.

And Victor clearly is not happy about our CI times. I could probably fill a whole talk about just CI. And that it's another point of the way we currently work did not catch up with all the things that we now need in this new day and age.

Artifacts, Prompts, and Agent-Driven Design

And I think CI, as it currently doesn't make any sense anymore. I'm currently experimenting with Codex. Maybe if we add intelligence, it could be more easier to decide which subset of the tests are actually useful.

But I feel that's a talk in itself and maybe something for another day. But if I keep scrolling up, it actually looks like Victor put a lot of thought into it. I was wrong.

This is actually really good. He basically took my work and then just fixed my stuff. This is awesome.

You know? Lunchtime crisis averted. Now, I give you a little bit of a tour.

We see our server less like an app but more like a place. there's a lot more that goes on when you build a project. It's not just about the code. So naturally, we have a lot of apps in the sidebar.

And some are dashboards and some are plugins.

Of course, there's nothing new as well. Like we used to have them. They were just scattered around on different servers.

Some used GitHub actions to update. There were databases. There were different repositories.

Like I didn't even know which one we all had. And clearly, it was not very inviting for the team to work on an update on these. Like I give you a simple one.

Because we were just talking about CI. So I made this dashboard that tracks how our CI times are. And clearly, we need to do more work.

But the beauty is, any time I want to tweak the dashboard, I can just tell the agent, make this blue. And it will not like me about this. And then we'll just update the dashboard as we go along.

Now, what are most dashboards really? It's like a session that generates some artifact. And then there's an automation that updates that session.

And of course, the artifact contains code. So, it's software in a way. But there's a better word now if you think about it.

We iterate so fast on things. Is it still software or is it jellyware? I like jellyware.

So let me show you a few other things. Of course, we have the community. Here we go.

We track all these numbers. How many PRs do we have? How many issues are reported?

How many are merged? Some people are really into graphs. We also do silly things on the server.

Like the daily Claw that tries to make sense of all the things that merge on the server. And then makes a newspaper out of it. And sometimes it's actually quite good.

But many times it's very wrong. But it's just, you have to have fun when you build. That's the whole point if you want to do good work.

I also have a slop meter.

Because if you all work with agents, it's very easy to like agents generate more and more and more and more and more code until you're like in a bad place. So you should always like try to push the agent to clean up. And as you see, ever since I started the dashboard, I definitely raised awareness.

And things are moving in the right direction. Now these were all just HTML plugins. We also have some that are actual code.

Like if you go on reports. I'm a curious person. So I always want to see how busy is everyone.

And as you can see, the activity, how many commits do they do, how active they are on Discord. Now we also built meetings. And it looks like there's a meeting in progress right now.

We used to have our own software that we paid for until I was why do we pay for this?

This is a prompt. So we just made it a prompt. It uses Luna to summarize our transcripts.

And the agent just joins us in Discord whenever we have a meeting. And the coolest thing, but I'm not going to show you that today because we already angered the demo gods with voice, is our agent can now talk back. like just taking notes. That's nothing new.

But connect GPT Live. And then you can actually ask the agent about your work or spin off new work. And because it's the same identity that represents the server and the same main session that knows everything.

This works really well. Now, let's see who is actually online. If I go down there a little bit.

I love this view. And I'm always curious what Victor is up to. Because he usually takes my code and makes it pretty.

So it looks like Victor is working on some emoji stuff.

But I know he gave me a shot this morning. He told me that he made the sidebar nicer. Like I added this little view so you could see who is online, who is running.

But it doesn't look very good. So he told me he does it better. And then let me scroll through.

And the cool part is you can actually see how he works. And just seeing how he approaches his agents. And sometimes he uses very colourful language.

But he manages to squeeze out so many different design iterations. Let me scroll a little bit more so you see. Look at this.

He built whole editors to tweak this. And then he was still not happy. I think it's very hard to please Victor.

Oh, and then somebody else was joining in. And then they were collaborating together on this. There's more versions.

I don't even know which one we updated.

But eventually they found something that looks very compelling. And by the way, all these visualizations, they work in the Codex app as well. So if you're still stuck in the CLI, it's time to upgrade.

You're stuck in 2025. Even better, I know some companies that jump on a video call with a terminal. And then use that to talk to your agent.

There's a better way. Now, I want to give you a little bit of the broader vision here. Ultimately, what we are building here is an agent that builds our software.

This is kind of like the way to the software factory. And some of the work has to be very hands-on. You want to pair directly with an agent.

But I also run a lot of loops. So I use them to monitor feedback and then automatically land fixes. And some of those loops run on different machines.

Persistent Maintenance and Shared Experiments

And sometimes they stop or they need adjustment. And sometimes I wasn't even sure where on all my machines they were. Those loops need maintenance.

And also, ultimately, where do we still bring value? It's about taste. Taste is uniquely hard to describe.

It's often just a feeling. And that's not something I want to fully entrust on our agent. So this didn't really work well in the team.

Like, I was running too many. And slowly, one by one, we're moving all these loops to our team server so other people can learn. Because ultimately, we maintain the agent that builds our software.

Now, what types of loops do we run and how does that work? Like, I have a monitor that scans Discord, Twitter, and GitHub. I built little CLIs.

So this is very easy for the agent to get a lot of data. And then we categorize them.

And for certain categories, like update issues, the agent will read the report, will investigate. It will spin up a new test box to reproduce the error. If it can clearly reproduce it will come up with a fix.

It will see if it's fixed. And if all of that works, there's going to be another agent that reviews that work. And then your work can automatically land.

Now, what's the difference between a loop and a goal? So the loop basically keeps checking. This is something we do continuously.

I have another one for performance. We do another release of the team server every day. And then my update loop will detect that.

We'll take snapshots and we'll see if there's anything that regressed or it needs improvement. Now, if I do, slash goal, that work is towards a defined end state. Like right now, I have a goal that slowly, bit by bit, migrates the code base from synchronous SQLite to async database access.

We're still using SQLite here, but as the server grows and as we do more, we're thinking about maybe making the database itself swappable. So this has been running for 18 days. It's still running on my local Codex and it has landed over 100 PRs so far.

Over time, I want an agent per project. It should have its own memory, automations, goals, loops, and I can give it those high-level commands and it maintains and improves my software. Now, should we check back what people are building so far?

Who got lucky enough to actually use online? I see a few hands. Yeah, you were fast.

So here we go. And okay, we have the release radar here. We have...

Oh, this is a cool game. Okay. You don't mind me.

I'm just going to... What do you mean? Should the agent play? yes.

By now, agents are probably better, especially because this all supports CUA.

Ooh, island builder. Okay. What is this?

I have no idea how that works. What should we assure next? Okay.

Play Pictionary with the Claw. Name the concept. Can anyone else help me?

Who's online? Help me. Give me a hint.

Well, anyhow, I'll keep letting you play in the Explorer. And if you didn't get a spot, you can just download it and set it up on your own server. Again, it fully works with Codex.

We made sure it's a one-click to get your subscription included and you can play along. So, we've been showing you how a small team can work with agents together. And as more and more teams started using agents, we ran into another question.

How do you run, configure, and secure them all across an organization? And we definitely felt that pain. That's why we built an enterprise control plane.

And today, we are open sourcing it.

Deployment Controls and Scaling Agents

And with that, I'm going to bring up Kevin Lin. He's going to show you what we built. Hey, Kevin.

Hi, everyone. I'm Kevin Lin. And I lead OpenClaw Enterprise at OpenAI.

Now, OpenClaw Enterprise, or OCE in short, introduces an open source control plane to OpenClaw. It makes OpenClaw multi-tenant and adds governance and hard security boundaries to agent deployments. Now, we believe that a secure runtime is a necessary foundation for bringing persistent agents like dots and OpenClaw to everyone.

And so, today, I'll walk you through some of the security fundamentals that we've built into the platform. First, we enforce hard boundaries between trusted and untrusted workloads. This means that deterministic code runs in a separate container, and in our case, a separate cluster from where the agent is executing.

This prevents agents from changing their runtime. Second, we constrain what agents can do with sandboxing. We control their network access, what files they can write to, and what repositories they push to.

This lets us give agents useful tools without giving them access to everything. Next, we add model-based reviews on top of our existing controls. We use auto-review, which is a feature in both Codex and OpenClaw that uses another model to review the agent's actions and block potentially dangerous ones before they execute.

And finally, agents run as their own identities with dedicated service accounts and configurable connectors. This means that agents aren't impersonating users. They are themselves persistent entities.

They can be independently controlled, audited, and if needed, turned off.

Permissions and Community Agent Demonstrations

Now, it's these controls that have helped us scale our internal OpenClaw deployments to over 400 Claws. They work around the clock, fixing code, doing experiments, analyzing data, and escalating security concerns. So now, I'm going to show you guys what that looks like.

This is a hard Pictionary game. I don't know what that is. Okay.

Because we are unveiling OC to the world today, let's create a community agent. What you're seeing right now are presets. Presets are configurable agent bundles that an organization can configure so that agents are launched with your security best practices.

Let's call our agent Fred. For Fred, we're setting up with the Codex harness. We're going to give him a service account.

We're going to give Fred read-only access to the code base so that he can answer questions.

So let's bring Fred forth. Now, while Fred is coming online, I want to switch to another agent that we have, Cooper. So Cooper is a software agent.

And think of him as a persistent teammate. He helps us triage issues, solve bugs, and merge features end to end. Now, the OCE console, it's functional, but it's a bit plain.

So let's spice it up. Cooper, can you add a heat map of token usage per agent to the dashboard? Now, software agents are one of the most popular agents that we deploy.

inside of OpenAI. In fact, if you've submitted a Codex issue any time within the last month, there's a good chance that an OpenClaw has triaged it, reproduced it, and in many cases, merged it end to end. All right.

So Cooper is working. And a lot of what Peter talked about today is the future of work and multiplayer. Every agent that is deployed with OCE comes with that built-in.

So here is Cooper's dashboard. And I can open up an authenticated session to Cooper's team server. Let's see.

Okay. Perfect. Now, here you can see the conversation I just had, and you can further steer the conversation to precisely define how you want the feature to be created.

Make sure dashboard has custom color palettes. And teammates can also sign into the same session to either follow along or steer it. the web console.

All right. Now, while Cooper is working, I think Fred should be ready now. So let's check out the community page.

Hi, Fred. What are we launching today? It's not every day I get to message this Peter.

So I'm wondering what other messages I can send. Right now, what Fred is doing is he's looking for Linear issues, looking through Slack, and then using that context to answer this question. Ideally, in the next 10 seconds, or we're going to work, or we're going to go onwards.

We have a big Linear board. Okay. We got a reply.

Oops. I think we have some plug-in issues. But it does look like we got the OpenClaw release notes.

Well, we have a Linear issue for today. And the issue for today is launching OCE. So, Fred, please do better next time.

I'm going to recap. So, today we are launching OpenClaw Enterprise.

ClawLabs and Open-Source Infrastructure

This is a vendor-neutral open source platform for managing and deploying agents. Similar to how Kubernetes was the standard for deploying containers in the cloud, we envision OCE to do the same for agent deployments. We first started OCE at OpenAI, and we donated it to the OpenClaw Foundation early in its development.

There, we've continued building it with partners like Red Hat and NVIDIA. And today, we're opening it up to the world. Try it out.

Tell us how we can make it better. And help us build a secure foundation for agents. Thank you.

Back to you, Peter. Hey, thank you, Kevin. I want to come back to where we started.

OpenClaw can use Codex under the hood because Codex is open source. We also expanded the Codex open source program so more people have access to AI. And through Patch the Planet, we're working with groups like Trail of Bits to make open source more secure.

Open source is critical infrastructure, and part of the ambition here is to fix a whole class of vulnerabilities. That's how we're building OpenClaw with OpenClaw today. If you're trying shared agent workflows with your own team, especially larger ones, I'd love to hear what's working and what isn't.

Come find me after the talk. Thank you.
aiSummary: ClawLabs 演示多人共享的持久智能体工作流，并介绍结合协作、维护循环与可执行部署边界的开源控制平面 OpenClaw Enterprise。
oneSentenceSummary: ClawLabs 演示多人共享的持久智能体工作流，并介绍结合协作、维护循环与可执行部署边界的开源控制平面 OpenClaw Enterprise。
summary: ClawLabs 介绍团队如何从终端编码会话迁移到 Codex Desktop、分布式测试机器，最终转向共享的持久智能体服务器。更多算力并未消除由人替同事和智能体传话的瓶颈；团队可见的会话让代码变更背后的意图得以共享，也让贡献者能一起引导工作。现场通过共同修改游戏，以及追溯原始对话来理解评审变更，展示了这种协作。服务器还承载仪表板、会议摘要、设计迭代和维护自动化。讲者区分了持续检查的循环与具有明确终点的目标：修复流程先复现问题、验证修复，再由另一个智能体审核；此外还有性能回归检查，以及据称持续十八天、产出百余 PR 的数据库迁移目标。Kevin Lin 随后介绍开源多租户控制平面 OpenClaw Enterprise，其控制包括把受信任运行时代码与智能体执行隔离，限制网络和文件访问，使用模型审查行动，并为智能体分配独立服务账号。社区智能体获得仓库只读权限，向 Linear 写入时需团队批准；软件智能体则负责修改仪表板。团队称内部部署了四百余个 Claw，并将平台定位为与 OpenClaw Foundation 和合作伙伴共同开发的厂商中立基础设施。插件问题和生成摘要不准确等现场限制为愿景补充了边界；部署规模与效率主张没有独立评估。

mainPoints.point: 共享会话消除人工传话的瓶颈
mainPoints.explanation: 增加机器提升了处理能力，却让同事继续依赖一个人。共享服务器让对话和提示词可见，使协作者能理解意图、引导会话，并知道为什么要做某项修改。

mainPoints.point: 工作成果成为协作与持续更新的界面
mainPoints.explanation: 团队服务器整合仪表板、插件、会议摘要和设计实验。智能体在创建这些成果的同一会话中更新它们，共享对话也帮助减少相互冲突的工作。

mainPoints.point: 循环与目标分别组织持续维护和有终点的工作
mainPoints.explanation: 循环不断监测反馈或性能，目标则推进到明确的最终状态。问题修复案例要求复现、验证修复和另一个智能体审核；数据库迁移据称运行十八天，合入了百余 PR。

mainPoints.point: 智能体部署需要硬边界与独立身份
mainPoints.explanation: OpenClaw Enterprise 隔离确定性运行时代码与智能体执行，限制网络和可写资源，增加基于模型的行动审核，并分配服务账号。这些控制支持独立审计和停用，而非冒用用户身份。

mainPoints.point: 权限受限的社区智能体展示控制平面的治理方式
mainPoints.explanation: Fred 获得仓库只读访问，向 Linear 写入需团队批准；Cooper 通过共享的认证会话处理软件任务。团队称内部有四百余智能体，并强调平台开源和厂商中立，也承认现场出现了插件问题。

keyQuotes: 我评审过许多 PR，知道改了什么，却不知道为什么。
这能防止智能体修改自己的运行时。
它们可以被独立控制、审计，并在必要时关闭。
这是一个厂商中立的开源平台，用于管理和部署智能体。
